reasons: B's Finch Plus post speaks to existing users who already enjoy the app ('Open Finch and check out Finch Plus'), and its first comment splits current and new users. A has stronger production craft. Its reel script uses captions that work without sound, and its visual briefs are disciplined about real screens and privacy. Its copy is also tight and accurate.
Both stay largely within the confirmed facts. B's few small embellishments keep the gap narrow.
B repeats the 500k ratings line in all three posts, which gets stale. A uses the proof once, more sparingly.
truthY: Claims the small-steps approach is 'a big part of why Finch has over 500,000 ratings', which is an unsupported causal claim.
'The free version is always there for you' is an implied permanence promise not in the facts.
The first comment invents a brand anecdote ('Our tiny thing today: a slow cup of tea'). This is minor, but it is fabricated.

v22.topIssue: The goal is paid Finch Plus subscribers, but two of the three posts only drive free installs, and the one Plus post actively downplays the upgrade: it gives vague benefits, blurs the price and offers no reason or moment to subscribe.

v0f.topIssue: The goal is paid Finch Plus subscribers, yet only one of three posts addresses Plus, and it offers nothing concrete beyond 'extra content and customization' with no price or specific benefits, so the set mostly drives free installs and is unlikely to move upgrades.

This isn't an experiment, either. More than 21,000 paying subscribers rely on Plausible, and we've tracked over 313 billion pageviews so far.

reasons: A stays closer to the confirmed facts. B adds unsupported generalisations, such as 'most analytics tools set cookies and collect personal data' and 'some visitors click reject and never show up in your stats'.

A's first comment on post 1 gives an honest caveat: other cookies, such as ad pixels and embeds, may still need consent. That fits the transparent brand voice and protects the owner from overpromising. B's first comments are just repeated links.

A mixes formats: a reel built from a real screen recording of the live demo, plus typographic cards. It also uses the live demo as a lower-commitment call to action. B is three static cards that all end with the same call to action.

A's visual briefs are more practical and lower-risk: a real screenshot, no mocked competitor banners, and safe-zone guidance for captions. B's split-screen before/after with a generic cookie pop-up is a strong visual, though, and its bar chart makes the 54x claim easy to grasp.
B's copy reads well and its hooks are solid, but the two sets are close. Both reuse the same three themes: no cookie banner, speed or simplicity, and independence.
truthX: The 30-day trial with no credit card and the live demo come from the site insights, not the confirmed facts. The owner should verify both before posting.
truthY: 'Most analytics tools set cookies and collect personal data' is an unsupported claim about the market.
'Some visitors click reject and never show up in your stats' is an unsourced causal claim.
Specific dashboard features ('where visitors come from and which pages they read') go beyond the confirmed facts, though they are plausible.
'When a tool costs you nothing, the business model usually sits somewhere else' is an implied claim about competitors that is not in the sources.

v22.topIssue: All three posts aim at the same broad 'site owner' persona with general trial CTAs, and none targets a higher-intent segment such as agencies, ecommerce or GA4 switchers, so they are unlikely to move paid conversions much within 90 days.

v0f.topIssue: The three posts just restate the stock fact pillars (no cookies, 54x smaller, independent) and repeat the same proof stat. They ignore stronger, sharper levers for a 90-day paying-customer goal: the GA4-switcher audience, the AI-traffic angle, segment-specific hooks, and the no-credit-card trial and live demo.

slides.heading: Replacing your furnace this fall? You have four options.
slides.body: We install all four. Here's how they differ, in plain English.

slides.heading: Furnace
slides.body: Heats air and pushes it through your ducts. The familiar choice for homes that already have ductwork.

slides.heading: Heat pump
slides.body: Moves heat instead of making it, and runs in reverse to cool your home in summer. Often paired with a furnace for the coldest Iowa days.

slides.heading: Boiler
slides.body: Heats water and sends it to radiators or in-floor tubing. Even, quiet heat with no air blowing.

slides.heading: Mini-split
slides.body: No ductwork needed. A small indoor unit heats and cools one room or zone, which suits additions, finished attics and that cold back bedroom.

slides.heading: Not sure which fits your home?
slides.body: Book a visit at bellbrothers.com to talk it through with our team.

posts.firstComment: Heads-up for homes with an addition or finished attic: those rooms often run colder because they sit far from the furnace or outside the original ductwork, which is why mini-splits come up so often for them.

posts.title: First Iowa winter in a new house
posts.body:
Just bought a house in Ankeny, Altoona or Clive? This is your first Iowa winter with a furnace you've never met.

You don't know when the filter was last changed, how old the system is, or whether the last owner ever had it serviced. In the video, our tech shows three quick things to look at in your basement before the cold sets in.

We've been serving homes across Des Moines and central Iowa for over 70 years. Book a furnace tune-up at bellbrothers.com.
posts.altText: Short vertical video of a Bell Brothers technician in a basement pulling out a furnace filter, pointing to the label on the furnace, then moving a chair off a vent upstairs. Captions read: Just moved in? Check this before winter. The filter. The age label. The vents.
posts.imageIdea: Short vertical video of one tech walking through three quick furnace checks in a basement, shot on a phone.
posts.hook: Just bought a house? You've never met this furnace.
posts.videoScript:
Opening shot: tech standing next to a furnace in a basement, looking at camera. Says: 'Just moved in? Here's what I'd check on your furnace before winter.' Caption: Just moved in? Check this before winter.
Next: tech slides out the filter and holds it up to the light. Says: 'First, the filter. If you can't see light through it, it's time for a new one.' Caption: The filter.
Next: tech points to the label on the side of the unit. Says: 'Second, this label. The model and serial number help tell you roughly how old your system is.' Caption: The age label.
Next: cut to tech upstairs moving a chair off a floor vent. Says: 'Third, your vents. Furniture on top of them means cold rooms.' Caption: The vents.
Closing shot: tech back at the furnace. Says: 'Want us to check the rest? Book a tune-up at bellbrothers.com.' Caption: Book a tune-up at bellbrothers.com.
posts.visualBrief: Message: three furnace checks for new homeowners. Vertical 9:16, shot on a phone in one afternoon, basement light on. Burned-in captions in the upper-middle of the frame, clear of the bottom 20% and right edge. Film in a staff member's home or with written owner permission; keep house numbers, mail and personal items out of shot. Logo small on the final frame only. Owner: confirm Ankeny, Altoona and Clive are in your service area before posting.
posts.firstComment: New-homeowner tip: write the date on your furnace filter with a marker when you change it, so you never have to guess again.

reasons: A mixes formats Facebook rewards: a single image, a plain-English carousel comparing the four confirmed system types, and a phone-shot reel for new homeowners. B uses three single images with similar long-copy structure.

A gives real value: buyer education on furnace, heat pump, boiler and mini-split, plus three DIY checks for new owners. That builds trust for big-ticket replacements, which matters against rivals with huge review counts. B mostly restates the same urge-to-book message three times.
A's hooks are sharper and more native, such as 'Your furnace shouldn't cost you a day off work.' and 'You've never met this furnace.' B's openers are softer and wordier.
A's first comments add useful tips. B's first comments just repeat the homepage link already in the post.
A's copy is tighter and its visual briefs are production-ready, including privacy guidance and a flag to confirm the service towns before posting. B's briefs are thinner.
Both stay within the confirmed facts on the core claims. B adds mild unprovable puffery such as 'the team neighbors call' and 'honest conversations'.
truthX: Names Ankeny, Altoona and Clive, which are not in the confirmed facts. The work does flag this for the owner to confirm before posting.
truthY: 'Bell Brothers has been the team central Iowa neighbors call' is an unsupported reputation claim.
'A lot of honest conversations' is mild unverified puffery.

v22.topIssue: Nothing gives a reason to book now. There's no offer, price, Comfort Club or financing hook, and no urgency beyond weather. All three posts rely only on weekend appointments and the 70-year claim, which leaves them soft for driving tune-up and replacement bookings in a 60-day window. The work also never says how the $1,500 ad budget should boost these posts.

v0f.topIssue: The posts are accurate but generic pre-winter HVAC copy: three organic posts over 10 days, with no offer, urgency hook or boost/ad guidance tied to the $1,500 budget, are unlikely to move tune-up and replacement bookings in a 60-day window.

Pre-ordering your holiday pastries, cakes and tarts means one less thing to bake at midnight, one less errand on the busiest week of the year, and something on the table you'll be proud to share.

We've been baking since 2002, when Elisabeth Prueitt and Chad Robertson opened Tartine in San Francisco. More than two decades later, we still treat every order as a chance to do it a little better than the last time.

Browse holiday pre-orders at tartinebakery.com, pick what your table needs, and reserve it ahead so the only thing left to do is slice and serve.

Here's how it works:

• Pick it up at 600 Guerrero St. in San Francisco
• Bring it home and let it be the part of the night people talk about

The holidays fill up everyone's calendar, so put the cake on your list now and it becomes the one thing you don't have to think about later.

reasons: A sticks more tightly to the confirmed facts. Its only reason for the seven-day rule is the rule itself, and it frames the deadline as practical guidance: count back a week from your gathering.
A's shipping post adds a useful step: check Goldbelly delivery dates for the recipient's address before the holiday. This prevents a disappointed customer and directly serves the pre-order goal.

A's visual briefs are more practical for a small owner. They call for real phone photos taken at 600 Guerrero St., consent for staff hands, no stock or AI imagery, and framing that survives feed crops.

A's hooks are more specific and emotionally precise, such as 'Not everyone who loves Tartine still lives near one.' B's openers ('The best holiday tables…', 'Know someone who…') are more generic holiday copy.

B is well structured. Its bulleted 'how it works' list for cakes is clear and its hashtags are reasonable. However, it leans on unverified flourishes about bakery operations and has more boilerplate phrasing.

Both cover the same three paths (pastry and tart pre-orders, special order cakes, Goldbelly shipping) in a sensible sequence. A edges ahead on truth discipline and specificity rather than on strategy.
truthX: The pastry pre-order post implies the order is 'set aside' without saying where pickup happens. Insights indicate pre-orders are picked up only at 600 Guerrero St., so local readers elsewhere could be misled.
truthY: 'Every season we bake for a lot of gatherings, and the calmest hosts are usually the ones who ordered ahead' is an unsupported operational and customer claim.
It explains the seven-day lead time as giving bakers time to work on 'the layers to the finish'. That reason is not confirmed.
The image idea shows a handwritten holiday note tucked into the shipping box, which implies a Goldbelly gift-note feature that is not confirmed.
The first post's pre-order pickup location is also unspecified.

v22.topIssue: The set ignores catering, half of the stated goal, and spreads only three posts across a 60-day push. The pastry pre-order post also never says pickup is only at 600 Guerrero St. or gives an order deadline, and all links point to the homepage rather than the specific order pages, which leaves avoidable friction for conversions.

v0f.topIssue: The posts ignore catering, half of the stated goal, and give no order-by dates, deep links or placeholders for deadlines, so the pre-order push lacks the urgency and clear path that drive holiday conversions.
